reading.rtitle: Do Not Read the Clause Aloud
paras: At infrastructure conferences, there is a moment that investors have learned to dread. A lawyer puts a clause on the screen and reads it aloud, word for word: the Concessionaire shall, provided that the Grantor, in the event of. The room goes quiet, and not because people are listening. The audience can read faster than any speaker, and by the second line most of them are looking at their phones.

The lawyers who keep the room do something different. They never read the clause. They point at it and say what it means, in the language of a conversation. Shall becomes has to. Provided that becomes as long as. In the event of a breach becomes if the operator does not do it. And the Grantor and the Concessionaire become what everybody calls them in real life: the state and the operator.

This is not simplification. The rule stays exactly as precise as it was on the page, with the same conditions and the same exceptions. Only the register changes. Experienced speakers say that a good explanation answers four questions in under a minute: who has to do what, by when, and what happens if they do not. Anything that does not answer one of those questions can wait for the written materials.

The hardest part, for lawyers who work in a second language, is giving up the safety of the text. Reading feels precise, and paraphrasing feels like a risk. But a paraphrase that the audience understands is more precise, in practice, than a perfect quotation that nobody follows.
reading.source: A composite of advice given to legal speakers at infrastructure conferences, written for this lesson.

listenings.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining the second panel. Before we start, a word about the format, because it is a little different this year. Each panelist will see one real clause on the screen, from a contract or a regulation in their country. They will have sixty seconds to explain it. One request to our panelists: please do not read the clause aloud. The audience can read it on the screen, and most of them read faster than we speak. Tell us what it means. Who has to do what, and what happens if they do not. Our audience today is mostly investors and engineers, not lawyers, so imagine you are explaining it to a smart friend over coffee. After the sixty seconds, the floor is open for questions.

When I was at the agency, we had a simple test before we published any new rule. We gave the draft to one person outside the agency, an engineer or a journalist, and we asked them to explain the rule back to us in one minute. If they could not, the rule was not ready. Not the law, the words. Over the years I learned that every explanation has to answer three questions. Who has to do what. By when. And what happens if they do not. People sometimes say that plain language means simple law. It does not. The rule stays exactly as precise as before, with every condition and every exception. Only the words change. Shall becomes has to. Notwithstanding becomes even if. And suddenly the people who have to follow the rule can actually understand it.
